_comment: Single source of truth for the astrophysical ladder, read by server/game/levels.py and client/js/levels.js. min_mass = game mass where the level starts; real_kg = real-mass range shown in the HUD (mapped log-linearly within the level); top_mass = game mass that maps to the top of the last level's real range.

levels.name: Dust
facts: Space is full of tiny dust grains, many smaller than a speck of flour. Planets are built from dust like you!
In space, dust grains stick together into bigger and bigger clumps. Keep eating!

levels.name: Asteroid
facts: Asteroids are rocky leftovers from when the planets formed, about 4.6 billion years ago.
Most asteroids in our Solar System orbit in the Asteroid Belt, between Mars and Jupiter.

levels.name: Dwarf planet
facts: Pluto was called a planet until 2006. Now it is a dwarf planet, like Ceres and Eris.
A dwarf planet is big enough to pull itself round, but it hasn't cleared other objects out of its path.

levels.name: Terrestrial planet
facts: Terrestrial planets like Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars have solid, rocky surfaces.
Earth is the only planet we know of with oceans of liquid water on its surface.

levels.name: Gas giant
facts: Gas giants are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. There is no solid ground to stand on!
Jupiter is so big that about 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

levels.name: Brown dwarf
facts: Brown dwarfs are 'failed stars': too heavy to be planets, but too light to shine by fusing hydrogen.
Brown dwarfs glow faintly in infrared light because they are still warm from when they formed.

levels.name: Main-sequence star
facts: You're a star! Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. Our Sun is a main-sequence star.
Small stars glow red and can live for trillions of years. Big stars glow blue and burn out in a few million.

levels.name: Giant star
facts: When a star runs low on hydrogen in its core, it swells into a giant. If Betelgeuse replaced the Sun, it would reach past Mars!
Giant stars are enormous but not very dense: their outer layers are thinner than the air you breathe.

levels.name: Neutron star
facts: BOOM! Big stars end in a supernova explosion that blasts most of their mass into space. The crushed core left behind is a neutron star.
A neutron star is only about 20 km across, yet a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes.
Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times a second and sweep beams across space like a lighthouse. We call them pulsars.

levels.name: Black hole
facts: Too heavy! Your core collapsed into a black hole. Its gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
Black holes are tiny for their mass: one as heavy as the Sun would be only about 6 km across. The glowing disk around it is much bigger.
Heavy objects bend light. This is called gravitational lensing. Watch the grid bend around you!

levels.name: Quasar
facts: A quasar is a giant black hole swallowing gas so fast that its hot disk outshines a whole galaxy.
Quasars are among the brightest things in the universe. We can see them billions of light-years away.

levels.name: Galaxy
facts: Quasars shine in the centres of young galaxies. Now you're a whole galaxy: billions of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity!
Our Milky Way has a few hundred billion stars and a giant black hole at its centre called Sagittarius A*.
There are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the universe we can observe.
